content: Breath-holding attacks are a common phenomenon observed in children. Iron supplementation has been proposed as a potential intervention to reduce both the frequency and severity of these episodes. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of iron supplementation on the occurrence and intensity of breath-holding attacks in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, up to April 2009. References from included studies were also reviewed, and pharmaceutical companies producing oral iron supplements, as well as some trial authors, were contacted to identify any unpublished data or trials. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared iron supplementation with either a placebo or no treatment in children under 18 years of age who experienced recurrent breath-holding episodes (defined as more than three episodes). These episodes had to be reported by an observer. The primary outcomes assessed were the reduction in the frequency of breath-holding attacks over time and the reduction in their severity, such as the cessation of loss of consciousness or convulsive movements. Two independent reviewers selected the studies and extracted the relevant data. When necessary, study authors were contacted to provide missing information. The risk of bias in the included studies was evaluated using a domain-based approach. In cases of low heterogeneity among the studies, a fixed-effect meta-analysis was performed, and the results were presented as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Two trials, involving a total of 87 children, met the inclusion criteria. The findings from these trials demonstrated that iron supplementation significantly reduced the frequency of breath-holding attacks in children. The pooled odds ratio for this effect was 76.48 (95% CI: 15.65 to 373.72; P < 0.00001). A separate meta-analysis focusing on the complete resolution of breath-holding attacks with iron supplementation also showed a significant effect, with an odds ratio of 53.43 (95% CI: 6.57 to 434.57; P = 0.0002). The authors concluded that iron supplementation, administered at a dose of 5 mg/kg/day of elemental iron for 16 weeks, appears to be effective in reducing both the frequency and severity of breath-holding attacks in children. This intervention is particularly beneficial for children with iron deficiency anemia, as the response to treatment correlates with improvements in hemoglobin levels. However, iron supplementation may also be helpful for children who are not anemic or who have low-normal hemoglobin levels. The authors emphasized the need for further high-quality randomized controlled trials to confirm the efficacy of iron supplementation in managing breath-holding attacks in children.
